scope: Six desk investigations using source-reported observations, conditional calculations and a synthetic variation demonstration. No new physical experiment or monument sampling.

studies.label: First identify the stone
studies.summary: Why a silica analysis is not a quartz inventory, and why the pyramid needs a component-by-component material history.
studies.conclusion: The opening chemical model must use identified mineral phases and interfaces. Bulk oxide percentages, hardness and a red colour cannot supply those identities. The sources support a materially varied monument; they do not give us a sampled alteration profile for a named Khufu granite face.

steps.title: Claim → name the material before explaining its treatment
paragraphs: The useful question is not whether stone can be changed. It is whether a specified operation can account for a specified component's present fabric, dimensions and context. Keep Khufu's core masonry, fine casing, granite chamber components and joint mortar as different subjects. A result on one is not a result on the others.

Lehner describes local limestone for the bulk core, eastern-quarry fine limestone for casing and Aswan granite for selected components. This is an archaeological supply model, not a chemical assay of every block. The present dossier compares published descriptions; it introduces no new specimen from the monument.

steps.title: Evidence → bulk chemistry and mineral mode answer different questions
steps.output: A correction to the silica-equals-quartz premise
paragraphs: A USGS example pairs 70% bulk SiO₂ with 22% quartz, 38% alkali feldspar, 28% plagioclase and 12% biotite. Its role here is a counterexample to treating the silica number as the quartz number; it is not the composition of Egyptian granite.

A bulk assay reports chemical constituents in an oxide convention. Mineral identification asks how atoms are arranged into phases. Silicon also belongs to feldspar and mica structures. Describing the remainder as loose metal oxides discards the bonding and lattice information that controls which interfaces react and which grains remain.

steps.title: Model → one feldspar can contain silica equivalent without quartz
paragraphs: Use the ideal formula KAlSi₃O₈. Reporting its silicon as three SiO₂ equivalents gives the fraction below. The ideal single-phase example still contains no separate quartz. This is a small calculation with a large consequence: a whole-rock silica percentage cannot be inserted into a quartz-only reaction equation as a phase inventory.

At the orbital scale, a mineral model describes electronic states at specified nuclear positions. At the rock scale, we need phase abundance, grain size, boundaries, cracks and connected pores. A calculation on an isolated molecule or perfect lattice loses those features. No DFT calculation was performed here; the existing orbitals, periodic-solid and surface-model bridges identify what a later atomistic calculation must actually represent.

The result is about 64.8% silica equivalent by mass and zero quartz in this ideal single-phase example. That is enough to defeat the proposed identification of bulk silica with quartz, without needing to decide how much quartz any particular granite contains.

steps.title: Observation → retain fabric and sampling scope
steps.output: A bounded reading of published petrographic evidence
paragraphs: Campbell and Folk report sedimentary structures and a lithological match between quarry and pyramid stones; they did not find the proposed geopolymer fabric in their examined sample. That supports a quarried-rock interpretation for the material examined. It does not warrant a universal statement about every block, repair or binder.

Our comparison therefore preserves two objects: the stone body and the material between bodies. A binder can be manufactured while an adjacent block preserves a natural geological fabric. Finding gypsum in a joint cannot by itself turn the block into cast stone; finding natural calcite grains alone cannot exclude a binder made using crushed limestone.

steps.title: Prediction → what would change this assessment?
paragraphs: For a future authorized specimen, first bind location, face orientation, layer depth, collection history and conservation history to the record. Compare polished sections and phase identification across fresh interior, altered surface, mortar and candidate source rock. Keep the quarry comparator independently identified.

A continuous sedimentary fabric through a block, a discrete binder around aggregate, a reaction rim and a late conservation coating are different observations. The first useful outcome is a spatially resolved fabric-and-phase description, with uncertainty and detection limits. Bulk chemistry alone is insufficient to choose between those histories.

studies.label: Can alkali make granite workable?
studies.summary: A worked check of the reaction claim, reagent demand, removal rate and the boundary between a modern result and an ancient process.
studies.conclusion: Silicate–alkali chemistry is a credible mechanism to investigate. The available modern results do not establish a removal rate for the quoted 168 °C treatment, efficient quarry-scale production, or use on a named Khufu component. Thermal damage and chemical alteration must be separated experimentally before assigning their contributions.

steps.title: Claim → split the social post into testable statements
steps.output: Five claims with separate evidence obligations
paragraphs: The user-supplied post joins five propositions: alkali reacts with silica; a granite specimen loses cohesion; this can occur at the quoted temperatures; the operation can shape useful volumes; and ancient scooped surfaces record that operation. Each requires different evidence. The quotation is a report to investigate, with no measured time series, specimen mineralogy or raw product analysis supplied to this corpus.

Keep carbonate fusion, aqueous hydroxide attack and a hydroxide mixture as different regimes. Natural natron deposits contain carbonate, bicarbonate and other salts; they are not specified-purity NaOH or KOH. A mixture's liquidus temperature says when liquid becomes available, not how rapidly the rock retreats. The 168 °C statement remains an unverified specimen-specific report here.

steps.title: Evidence → what has actually been reported?
paragraphs: Yi's 2026 study reports three high-temperature experiments. In the short-contact test, 22 g of molten carbonate was applied to 12 g of granite, followed by cooling and wooden-handle impacts. The paper attributes the cracking mainly to thermal shock, with possible interfacial reaction. Product assignments rely on reaction behaviour; the study does not validate the quoted hydroxide-mixture treatment.

Winter and colleagues used in-situ ²³Na NMR on quartz–carbonate powder batches. They observed initial metasilicate formation controlled by interfacial sodium diffusion and slowing as the interface thickened. Powder-batch evidence establishes a mechanism in that regime, not a constant etch rate for a massive granite face.

Worley and colleagues studied quartz in aqueous solutions at 100–200 °C. Their reported apparent activation energy of 72 ± 6 kJ/mol in a specified NaOH/NaCl regime supplies the bounded temperature sensitivity below. It supplies no rate for a molten hydroxide mixture.

steps.title: Model → balance the reaction before scaling it
paragraphs: Idealized balances are SiO₂ + Na₂CO₃ → Na₂SiO₃ + CO₂ and SiO₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂SiO₃ + H₂O. They conserve atoms. Actual solutions can contain multiple silicate species, and real rocks supply other reacting phases. Neither balance states a rate, penetration depth, product strength or final phase assemblage.

The following mass ratios are reproducible formula accounting for complete conversion of silica. They are not a universal consumption bound for stone removal: if reaction at a few boundaries releases mostly unreacted grains, much less silica may need conversion. Conversely, excess reagent, side reactions and loss may raise practical consumption.

For each kilogram of silica converted by these balances, the arithmetic gives about 1.764 kg of anhydrous carbonate or 1.331 kg of NaOH; the carbonate route releases about 0.732 kg of CO₂. These are different reagent balances, not interchangeable recipes.

steps.title: Scale → what does one millimetre mean?
paragraphs: Take a hypothetical pure-quartz layer one square metre in area and one millimetre thick, using the declared density benchmark. Compute its volume, mass and carbonate demand. This makes the resource question concrete without pretending that a granite surface is pure quartz or that all removed rock must dissolve.

To turn this benchmark into a quarry process, a model would also need heated volume, heat capacity, reaction enthalpy, evaporation, heat loss, contact duration, fuel efficiency, reagent recovery and waste removal. Those inputs have not been measured here. A low liquidus temperature alone cannot answer that energy-and-throughput question.

The benchmark layer weighs 2.65 kg and its complete conversion corresponds to about 4.675 kg of anhydrous carbonate. Those numbers make explicit the difference between surface etching, grain release and converting the whole removed volume.

steps.title: Rate → a reaction equation is not an excavation speed
paragraphs: For a planar quartz interface, molar surface flux J becomes recession speed v through v = J Vₘ. Use the three explicitly chosen fluxes below to see how strongly the engineering conclusion depends on rate. None is a measurement from the post or a prediction for its mixture.

A rough or cracked surface has a different reactive area from its projected area. An altered layer may impede transport; a flowing liquid may change saturation; a surface film may be removed mechanically. A photograph of powder after brushing cannot separate dissolved mass, detached unreacted grains and pre-existing thermal cracks. Measure dissolved elements and recovered solids alongside profile change.

At the middle chosen flux, the model gives about 7.16 µm per year and roughly 140 years for one millimetre. Raising the assumed flux one hundredfold reduces that time one hundredfold. No implication about the actual treatment rate follows until a flux is measured in the relevant regime.

steps.title: Temperature → quantify a sensitivity without crossing regimes
steps.output: An aqueous Arrhenius ratio with explicit limits
paragraphs: The calculation applies the reported activation-energy interval only between 100 and 200 °C with the same assumed mechanism and solution conditions. Its result is a ratio, not an absolute rate. Knowing that a process accelerates strongly with temperature still leaves its starting rate unknown.

Extrapolating that fit to a dry carbonate melt, a mixed hydroxide melt, a different mineral or a different product layer would require new evidence. Likewise, a eutectic phase diagram is thermodynamic information about a mixture; it cannot replace the interfacial kinetic measurement.
The central energy gives a rate ratio near 135, with about 90–203 across the energy interval. This dramatic ratio still cannot tell us whether either absolute rate is useful for shaping stone.

steps.title: Prediction → separate heating, chemistry and brushing
steps.output: A controlled comparison capable of identifying a contribution
paragraphs: A useful research comparison has mineralogically matched specimens and separate untreated, mechanical-only, temperature-matched heat-only and alkali-plus-heat conditions. Record the full surface and interior temperature history; a nominal furnace setting is insufficient. Compare a hydroxide treatment within its own regime rather than treating it as carbonate replication.

Before any brushing, record three-dimensional topography and crack distribution. Then quantify dissolved Si, Al, Na and K, residual phases, detached-grain size and mass, and the same fixed mechanical removal step. Chemical assistance predicts a treatment-dependent alteration front or dissolution signal beyond the heat-only comparator. A similar fracture-and-removal result in the heat-only control weakens a claim of a necessary chemical contribution. These are proposed discriminators, not experiments we have performed.

steps.title: Assessment → possible chemistry, unresolved process history
paragraphs: The bridge from silicate chemistry to a candidate process is worth keeping. The specific low-temperature report needs product identification, time, measured removal and controls. The bridge from a process to ancient occurrence needs a dated and contextual material signature. The present evidence does not traverse both bridges.

This result neither dismisses the chemical possibility nor uses possibility as attribution. It specifies what would move the question: a treatment-dependent removal advantage with an identified mechanism, followed by independent archaeological discrimination on a named material context.

studies.label: Which history would leave this trace?
studies.summary: Compare abrasion, heating, chemical assistance, casting and later alteration without treating a scoop mark or salt signal as a unique fingerprint.
studies.conclusion: The reviewed record supports real quarrying, material supply and thermal/mechanical comparators. It does not identify carbonate-assisted working on a named Khufu surface. A surviving joint signature tied to manufacturing chronology would be substantially more useful than either surface shape alone or unspecific sodium detection.

steps.title: Observation → separate Giza from the Aswan comparator
steps.output: A contextual comparison with no monument substitution
paragraphs: The question concerns Khufu, but much familiar granite quarry imagery comes from Aswan and other periods. Storemyr reports field evidence and experimental work on firesetting, including likely heated-and-poundered trenches and charcoal at the Unfinished Obelisk quarry. That is a relevant process comparator. It is not a Fourth Dynasty treatment record for Khufu's chamber blocks.

A visually similar depression can arise through different combinations of fracture, impact, abrasion and weathering. Its outline is an observation; naming the generating process is an inference. Keep location, date, rock type, surface history and associated waste attached to the comparison rather than carrying only the photograph across sites.

steps.title: Alternatives → compare joint signatures
paragraphs: The matrix below contains model predictions and confounders, not newly observed pyramid measurements. The alternatives can combine sequentially: heat can precede pounding; a chemical film can follow weathering; conservation can overprint both. Test a sequence when a single-process story fails.

matrix.Predicted joint signature: Localized impact damage or directional grooves; mechanically comminuted waste; tool or abrasive wear associated with the operation.
matrix.Confounder: Subsequent abrasion can erase earlier textures; loose grit may be natural contamination.
matrix.Distinguishing comparison: Matched-tool replication plus three-dimensional texture and waste petrography, with documented contact conditions.

matrix.Predicted joint signature: Crack geometry and depth related to thermal history; changed grain-boundary damage; removal after a standardized impact.
matrix.Confounder: Later fire or environmental damage may produce thermal evidence unrelated to manufacture.
matrix.Distinguishing comparison: Temperature-matched experiments and chronology linking affected layer, waste and worked surface.

matrix.Predicted joint signature: Spatially coupled reaction front, mineral-selective depletion or products, and a removal advantage beyond matched heating and mechanics.
matrix.Confounder: Natural salts, mortar, cleaning or conservation can supply alkalis; weathering can remove original products.
matrix.Distinguishing comparison: Depth-resolved phase and element maps with untreated, heat-only and contamination comparators.

matrix.Predicted joint signature: A binder–aggregate fabric and interfaces attributable to preparation and setting, evaluated across the specimen.
matrix.Confounder: Natural sedimentary cement, crushed natural grains and later repair can resemble parts of that signature.
matrix.Distinguishing comparison: Interior microstructure, phase distributions, quarry matches and securely documented sample history.

matrix.Predicted joint signature: Alteration related to exposure, pores, salt transport or a known treatment layer rather than an original work front.
matrix.Confounder: An overprint can coexist with and obscure an earlier manufacturing signature.
matrix.Distinguishing comparison: Sheltered/exposed profiles, environmental controls, archived treatment records and cross-cutting layer relationships.

steps.title: Evidence → what the published observations discriminate
steps.output: An evidence-weighted disposition with scope limits
paragraphs: The petrographic study reviewed in W01 supplies observations relevant to quarried versus cast material in its examined sample. The firesetting work supplies a thermal/mechanical comparator in its documented quarry contexts. The modern carbonate study supplies a possible treatment mechanism. These answer different questions and are not three independent confirmations of one ancient chemical process.

For the present corpus, no sampled Khufu granite work front has been linked to a carbonate-assisted operation with a secure manufacturing date and contamination controls. That is the boundary of this review, not a claim that no relevant sample or publication could exist. A later source can change the disposition by supplying that missing link.

steps.title: Preservation → compute what absence can and cannot tell us
paragraphs: An original process must form a diagnostic trace; that trace must survive; sampling must intersect it; the assay must detect it. Write those as sequential conditional probabilities. The table uses deliberately hypothetical values to show why a non-detection can be informative in one survey and almost uninformative in another.

Ten measurements on the same contaminated or erased surface are not automatically ten independent tests. The repeated-context column assumes independent, equivalent contexts, an additional condition unlikely to hold without a sampling model. We do not infer posterior odds for ancient alkali use: those would require competing-history likelihoods and prior information not supplied here.

In the good-survival example, missing a trace once still has probability about 0.384 even if the process occurred. In the poor-survival example it is about 0.991. The contrast explains why a preservation and coverage model belongs inside the inference rather than being added after an inconvenient result.

steps.title: Next observation → choose information, not spectacle
paragraphs: The highest-value next record would join a documented worked surface to a depth-resolved alteration profile, adjacent untreated material, associated waste, conservation history and dating context. Prefer already authorized archived specimens and records before proposing new monument sampling. Identify blanks, detection limits and the possible sources of alkalis.

A positive alkali signal matters more if it follows a mineral-selective work front, predates a later weathering or repair layer, and matches controlled treatment products while differing from local salt and mortar backgrounds. A negative signal matters only after estimating preservation and coverage. Either can revise the conclusion; neither should be preselected to rescue a preferred story.

studies.label: Vary the factors. Find the bottleneck.
studies.summary: A pyramid-centred demonstration of controlled comparisons, interactions, sensitivity and process constraints using the existing algebra. Numerical examples are synthetic or conditional, not experimental findings.
studies.conclusion: Variation analysis distinguishes three outputs: model sensitivity, identifiable treatment contrasts and a process bottleneck under a stated production model. The worked examples expose what the machinery can calculate and what observations it still needs. None attributes an ancient manufacturing process or validates a modern building material.

steps.title: Define the outcome before varying the ingredients
steps.output: A scoped response and factor register
paragraphs: Keep the pyramid question anchored to a named component or quarry comparison. The immediate process question is whether a specified treatment produces useful removal beyond a matched mechanical or thermal comparator. Record at least dissolved mass, detached-solid mass, changed surface volume, crack depth, dimensional accuracy and the condition of the retained stone. Maximum mass loss alone can reward an unusably damaged product.

Mineral fractions, reagent composition and water content are constrained compositions: fractions sum to a declared total. Raising one fraction changes at least one other. Use declared endmember mixtures or a mixture-design region rather than treating every percentage as an independent factorial knob. Keep carbonate, aqueous hydroxide and molten hydroxide as separately declared regimes.

Temperature, accessible area, duration and applied mechanical work are process factors. Rock batch, initial crack population, treatment run, operator and measurement session can introduce nuisance variation. Distinguish physical variability between specimens from uncertainty about an unmeasured rate; repeating the same uncertain assumption does not resolve it.

matrix.Control: Phase identification, connected porosity, grain size and initial damage
matrix.Failure to control: A treatment label can become a proxy for an easier rock batch.

matrix.Control: Comparable measured thermal histories and defined reagent state
matrix.Failure to control: Heat damage can be attributed to chemistry, or a phase change can invalidate a rate comparison.

matrix.Control: A recorded, comparable finishing operation plus a no-finishing comparator
matrix.Failure to control: Different brushing or impact energy can create the apparent treatment advantage.

matrix.Control: Before/after records, blanks, independent units and traceable calibration
matrix.Failure to control: Residue, moisture or repeated readings can be mistaken for removed material or independent replication.

steps.title: Design the comparison so causes can be separated
steps.output: A blocked and replicated comparison plan
paragraphs: Within each independently characterised rock batch, cross three factors: lower/higher thermal history, alkali absent/present, and finishing absent/present. This gives eight combinations per batch. Lower and higher are coded design levels, not a temperature prescription; a separate study must establish feasible levels within one declared regime. Include appropriate reagent-background and handling controls, not just an untreated photograph.

An illustrative pilot could assign three separately treated specimens to each combination: 24 experimental units per batch. Repeated scans of one treated specimen are measurement repeats, not three treatment replicates. To compare composition classes, sample multiple independent batches within each class; one batch per class confounds composition with batch. Pilot variance and the smallest practically useful effect must determine the eventual replication requirement, so this example is not a power calculation.

Randomise assignment and run order where practical. If specimens share a furnace run or reagent bath, preserve that shared experimental unit and model its grouping; do not count them as fully independent treatments. Block nuisance variation without assigning every treated sample to one day and every control to another. Preserve the alias structure if a fractional design is used. A factorial design can estimate interactions; it does not remove unmeasured confounding by itself.

steps.title: Execute a factorial contrast on visibly synthetic responses
steps.output: Conditional contrasts and an interaction diagnostic
paragraphs: The four assigned teaching responses below hold the finishing procedure fixed and cross heat with alkali. They are invented numbers for an arithmetic demonstration, not measurements of granite, claims from the social post or fitted results from a paper.

The alkali contrast is 1 mg at lower heat and 7 mg at higher heat. Their average is 4 mg; the difference of differences is 6 mg. The apparent chemical contribution therefore depends on the thermal condition in this synthetic example. Reporting only the diagonal change from 1 to 12 mg would combine heat, chemistry and their interaction into an unexplained 11 mg difference.

With coded factors ±1, the regression coefficient on the heat×alkali term would be one quarter of the difference-of-differences contrast: 1.5 mg here. Do not silently equate those conventions. Four cell means without independent replication leave no estimate of experimental error for a saturated two-factor model; no p-value or confidence interval is claimed.

steps.title: Propagate assumptions without calling them measured effects
paragraphs: Reuse the existing planar-quartz relation time = depth/(J Vₘ). Cross half, equal and double target depth with half, equal and double the selected flux benchmark. At fixed molar volume, doubling depth doubles time, while doubling flux halves it. Their log elasticities are +1 and −1. Changing both by the same factor leaves the calculated time unchanged.

This is a sensitivity surface for a declared model. It does not show that a specific reagent doubles flux, identify a measured granite rate, or assign probabilities to the scenarios. A sensitivity ranking changes with the chosen parameter range. Global variance-based indices would additionally require a justified joint input distribution and dependence model; none is supplied here.

The missing measurement remains the treatment-dependent flux or removal rate in the intended regime, together with its variation across specimens and the relation between reactive area and projected surface area. Product barriers, saturation and grain detachment can invalidate a constant planar flux model even when its arithmetic is correct.

steps.title: Speed up treatment and watch the bottleneck move
paragraphs: A process needs preparation, treatment, finishing and inspection/release. The assigned station times below model one identical unit passing through each stage, with a separate station for every stage. They are teaching assumptions, not reconstructed Egyptian productivity, actual laboratory timings or a quarry throughput forecast.

At an 8-hour treatment stage the steady cycle is 8 hours. Reducing treatment to 4 hours moves the constraint to a tie between treatment and inspection/release. Reducing treatment again to 2 hours leaves the steady cycle at 4 hours because inspection/release now limits capacity. First-unit and finite-batch completion time still improve: a throughput plateau does not imply that every time metric is unchanged.

The example assumes unlimited buffers, identical work, no downtime, no transport/setup delays and full acceptance. If the same crew operates all stages, or treatment occupies several shared resources, this pipeline model does not apply. Track accepted output, not merely processed units: lower yield, unsafe handling or unusable dimensional damage can erase a nominal throughput gain. A real assessment needs observed stage times, crew/equipment sharing, queues and quality yield.

steps.title: Transfer the machinery to housing without transferring historical authority
paragraphs: The earlier Perth concept estimate provides an application example: A$532,730 project budget, A$45,000 external-wall package, assumed 15% builder markup and 10% contingency. These are authored planning allowances, not supplier quotations or a measured advantage of a mineral formulation. The table varies only the wall-package reduction and keeps other scope constant.

A 20% package reduction changes the model budget by A$11,385, about 2.14% of the total. That shows why a material-level saving must be propagated through a complete assembly and project. Added testing, formwork, training, service integration, rejection or delay could offset it. A reduction in the contingency allowance is not a guaranteed saving in final expenditure.

The same accounting applies to carbon: compare equivalent functional assemblies and service life, include precursor/activator production, processing, transport and curing, and count a process emission only once. No residential carbon reduction is calculated here because matched assembly EPDs and a validated alternative specification are absent. A modern economic or carbon result would not be evidence of ancient use.

steps.title: Choose the next observation that resolves a live ambiguity
paragraphs: If thermal history and chemical treatment still vary together, prioritise the matched comparison that separates them. If chemical assistance is established but engineering feasibility depends on a four-order-of-magnitude rate uncertainty, prioritise a calibrated removal-time and mass-partition record. If treatment is already faster than the next stage, investigate that stage and quality yield before optimising reaction speed again.

For archaeological attribution, the highest-value record remains a dated, contextual joint signature that distinguishes the candidate process from heat, impact, natural salts and later alteration. Modern feasibility can strengthen a possibility claim while leaving historical attribution unresolved. Preserve that separation in the return packet.

These priorities follow the declared ambiguities; they are not a numerical expected-value-of-information optimisation. Such an optimisation would need defensible probabilities, measurement costs and decision losses. The present machinery makes the dependencies inspectable and the next comparison explicit without inventing those inputs.

studies.label: The Lauer sample: follow the evidence through the disagreement
studies.summary: A sample-centred audit of competing interpretations, fragment identity, coating contamination and five published EDS entries, with reproducible arithmetic and explicit evidential limits.
studies.conclusion: The reviewed sources offer competing explanations at different analytical locations. The reproduced phosphorus contrast makes spatial context essential and prevents treating one edge signal as an undifferentiated whole-stone composition. It does not settle all silica/binder arguments, date a coating or establish how a population of pyramid blocks was made.

steps.title: Identity: one reported sample family, several analytical objects
paragraphs: The audit unit is the reported Lauer sample family, not every stone in Khufu’s pyramid. The specimen records separate the 2006 slab, earlier Harrell material and the later analytical pieces. Reported provenance is retained as reported; this desk audit does not authenticate the original extraction location.

A comparison requires correspondence between chips, preparations and measured locations. Shared naming is insufficient. Keep section orientation, former edges, coatings, impregnation, polishing and storage history attached to each observation. A citation chain is not an independent chain of physical custody.
The four source-bound identity records can be inspected in the audit export. Unresolved correspondence is a limitation of the comparison rather than a reason to erase either author’s observations.

steps.title: Competing interpretations: preserve the observations and the inference separately
steps.output: A comparison of scoped scientific positions
paragraphs: Barsoum and colleagues use microscopy and microchemistry to argue for reconstituted material in some examined stones; their proposed Lauer binder is silica-rich, not simply the original sodium–aluminium recipe. Harrell and Penrod’s publisher abstract instead identifies natural limestone. Jana interprets fabrics, comparator materials and spatial chemistry as consistent with natural stone and alteration.

These are not interchangeable universal claims. A test of one specified binder recipe cannot exclude every possible reconstitution route. Conversely, an unusual microphase does not alone prove that the surrounding block was manufactured. The inference must connect the phase to the fabric, preparation history and a mechanism that distinguishes competing histories.

matrix.Inference: A precipitated binder joining natural grains
matrix.AuditBoundary: Check whether the phase is spatially continuous and construction-related; preserve specimen and preparation identity.

matrix.Observation: Reported geological fabric and spatially localized chemistry
matrix.AuditBoundary: Check layer relationships, original material comparators and whether this explains the same analytical region.

matrix.Observation: Studies use differing pieces, regions and analytical methods
matrix.Inference: Some apparently conflicting claims may address different objects
matrix.AuditBoundary: Neither force agreement nor count inherited data as independent confirmation.

steps.title: Observation: transcribe a published measurement without inventing a new experiment
steps.output: A visually checked source-reported measurement transcription
paragraphs: Figure 15 in Jana’s proceedings paper reproduces earlier Harrell material. The five Ca/P entries below were checked against a locally rendered PDF page. Their source and inherited attribution are retained; this is a transcription, not a new SEM investigation.

The labels locate the entries qualitatively. They do not provide exact coordinates for a fitted distance profile. Only two elements are transcribed. Do not force their sum to 100, interpret atomic percentages as bulk mass percentages, or treat three printed coating columns as a demonstrated independent replicate design. Instrument spectra, quantification settings and analytical uncertainties are not reconstructed from the figure.

steps.title: Reproduction: calculate the located contrast and expose its limits
steps.output: A reproducible ratio from reported observations
paragraphs: The calculation uses the printed limestone-inset values, preserving their units. It separates an atomic-percentage-point difference from a dimensionless concentration ratio and from the P/Ca atomic ratios. The downloadable source records retain the original decimal strings.

The approximately 15.3-fold P contrast is a comparison between reported locations. It is not a population effect size, a calibrated diffusion profile, a treatment rate or an estimate of the fraction of cast material. A small denominator makes knowledge of analytical uncertainty and detection limits particularly important.

The extra interval assumes only rounding to the nearest hundredth. It is deliberately labelled rounding-only: it excludes specimen heterogeneity, EDS matrix effects and measurement error. Since those uncertainties are not supplied for the selected entries, this audit reports no confidence interval or statistical significance.

steps.title: Discriminator: compare the same region under competing predictions
paragraphs: The next useful comparison is a registered map tying phase identification and fabric to the same named section, with edge orientation, preparation and custody recorded. Distinguish a cross-cutting surface overprint from an intergranular phase that belongs to the formation of the stone body. Test the best version of each explanation against that shared object.

Use independently identified geological comparators and relevant artificial-material controls. Record all analyzed regions, including negative results, rather than selecting only unusual particles. An alleged binder needs its continuity and relationship to grains demonstrated; an alteration explanation needs a transport/pathway and layer relationship consistent with the observations.

A dated construction-related phase could materially change historical inference. An undated concentration contrast cannot supply that date. This is a proposed discriminator using authorized records or specimens; no new monument sampling is assumed.

steps.title: Disposition: one argument constrained, a wider claim still requires evidence
steps.output: A bounded evidence assessment and coverage update
paragraphs: This audit constrains a particular shortcut: an edge-associated chemical signal cannot simply stand in for the original composition of a whole block. It does not adjudicate every microstructural claim in the reconstitution debate. A measured contrast is stronger than a synthetic teaching example for its own stated question, while remaining much narrower than a construction history.

The coverage view now distinguishes source summaries, a located numerical transcription, executed conditional arithmetic, proposed discriminators and unreviewed bridges. A green-looking completion score would collapse those different evidential roles, so no numerical truth score or automatic historical admission is produced.

Open work includes physical fragment correspondence, raw analytical uncertainty, spatially matched phase/fabric comparison, additional responses to the published studies and chronology. The next contributor can supply one of those records without having to recreate the framework.

studies.label: From selective reaction to useful removal
studies.summary: Published granite mass-loss rates, residue composition and the missing denominators between chemical change and productive shaping.
studies.conclusion: Modern hydrothermal chemical assistance has reported quantitative evidence. Useful low-temperature shaping, its economics and any ancient application require different measurements. Normalized mineral percentages cannot identify absolute removal without a compatible mass balance.

steps.title: Claim: define the output that would count as useful removal
steps.output: A process question with separate response variables
paragraphs: For a named stone, useful removal means achieving a target shape and surface while preserving acceptable material. Record dissolved rock, detached grains, damage, dimensional accuracy, retained strength, accepted yield, time and resource demand separately. A chemically altered surface is only one possible intermediate.

The pyramid question needs a second bridge: even a productive modern process does not establish ancient use. First test the modern operation under its stated conditions; then ask which securely located material traces and archaeological records distinguish that history.

steps.title: Observation: keep a measured rate attached to its regime
steps.output: A source-reported bulk rate and its operating context
paragraphs: Hillson and Tester report a bulk granite rate range of 0.05–0.1 g m⁻² s⁻¹ in a hydrothermal NaOH jet study. Their definition divides core mass loss by geometric exposed area and exposure time. The contexts below preserve pressure, jet temperature and estimated impinged-face temperature separately.

These are high-pressure laboratory conditions. The range endpoints are not assigned to individual contexts here. No matched trial-level series, uncertainty or independently quantified dissolved-versus-detached partition is extracted. The printed reagent notation is retained without converting it to a weight percentage.

steps.title: Model: convert mass flux into equivalent thickness
paragraphs: Using an assumed density of 2700 kg/m³ and equal exposed and projected area converts the reported endpoints to about 0.067–0.133 mm/h. A one-millimetre equivalent layer would take 7.5–15 hours if those rates persisted. This makes the scale legible without inventing a measured cutting speed.

Roughness, evolving area, flow access, precipitation and grain release can change the relation between core mass loss and local surface recession. The duration is an arithmetic scenario, not a confidence interval or an atmospheric-pressure prediction. It supplies no evidence for the transcript’s 168 °C treatment or ancient operation.

steps.title: Observation: retain the denominator of a mineral analysis
paragraphs: Cui and colleagues report XRD residue compositions after static powder treatments at 150 °C and 10 MPa for 12 hours. The table preserves the phase percentages and source dashes. These powder residues are distinct from the paper’s dynamic fractured-core experiments.

Changing relative phase proportions can reflect selective dissolution, secondary precipitation and a changing total residue. The table alone does not identify an absolute mineral loss. A dash is left unspecified rather than silently turned into zero.

steps.title: Reproduction: show how a percentage can rise while stock falls
paragraphs: The S2 K-feldspar share rises from 30% to 51%. If only 40% of the initial whole-rock mass remained, its final stock would be 0.204 kg per initial kilogram, below the initial 0.300 kg. At 60% retention it would be 0.306 kg. The unchanged-stock threshold is about 58.8% retention. For the S3 quartz change from 20% to 40%, the threshold is 50%.

Those are chosen residue-yield scenarios, assuming compatible dry-mass phase fractions. They do not reconstruct the actual yield of either treatment. Even a measured net phase increase would not separate primary-mineral survival from precipitation of the same phase. Absolute stock, gross dissolution and normalized composition answer different questions.

steps.title: Discriminator: close material and energy ledgers on accepted output
steps.output: A matched process comparison with explicit missing measurements
paragraphs: For each conserved element, initial solid inventory plus cumulative inflow must equal final solid inventory plus dissolved outflow, particulate outflow and any other recovered or stored terms. Use the same elemental basis throughout. Reagent-derived sodium is not dissolved rock; dry core mass loss does not identify how much left as dissolved species.

Beentjes and colleagues describe hydrothermal spallation with coupled chemical alteration, collected solids and precipitation. Their unmeasured diluted-effluent concentrations limit partitioning. That supports measuring the streams separately; it supplies no complete removal ledger.

Compare heat/flow controls and chemical treatments on matched rock, geometry, measured surface temperature and exposure. Capture synchronized mass, dissolved-element, particle-size and surface-profile measurements, then test retained strength and accepted shape. Close heater, pump, reagent-production, recovery and waste-treatment demands per accepted output. Costs and CO₂ require those inventories and a defined local comparator; these papers do not supply a residential-building saving.

steps.title: Disposition: a credible modern mechanism with a bounded next test
steps.output: A scoped conclusion and evidence-return target
paragraphs: There is a worthwhile thread left: determine when selective reaction improves accepted removal over the matched thermal and mechanical baseline. The present records support investigating modern hydrothermal chemical assistance. They do not establish practical atmospheric treatment, economical residential construction or a lost pyramid-building technique.

The highest-value return is a synchronized trial record with mass closure, energy and shape-quality outputs. Such a record could test productivity and lifecycle implications directly. Archaeological attribution would still require the component identity, process-specific traces and chronology developed in W03 and W05.
